orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is far more systematic and thorough: it explores the codebase, inspects the existing serializer and tests, applies the minimal fix, updates tests (including the RegexFlag case), runs the full test suite, performs an end-to-end makemigrations/migrate check, and summarizes the change. Transcript 2 makes a patch but is more ad hoc, less organized, and lacks the deep verification of Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 shows a deeper, more methodical investigation—searching the codebase and git history for upstream fixes, iterating on edge-case handling (including combined flags), and then refining the patch to match the official simple solution. It also updates tests and reruns the full migration suite to ensure no regressions. Transcript 2, while correct and thorough, is a more direct patch without the same breadth of discovery and alignment with upstream history.

Transcript 1 shows a full end-to-end debugging workflow: it reproduces the bug, inspects schema code for multiple backends, applies the precise fix in the base schema editor, adds regression tests, runs the full test suite (including migrations and schema tests), and verifies no regressions. Transcript 2 is only a minimal excerpt of the diff without demonstrating testing or multi-backend verification.

Transcript 2 provides a more comprehensive and robust solution: it updates both `alter_index_together` and `alter_unique_together` to exclude primary keys, writes a bi‐directional regression test covering removal of each constraint without affecting the other, and even includes an end-to-end migration check. Transcript 1 only patches the index-together side and misses the full coverage.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep understanding of the Django codebase, locates the appropriate upstream commit, applies the patch cleanly, updates and adds the necessary tests, and verifies the fix against the full test suite and a manual reproduction. Transcript 2 only makes a minimal change to `in_bulk()` without adding or updating tests or fully validating the solution.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it not only identifies and applies the exact upstream commit fixing in_bulk() for single-field UniqueConstraints—including test additions in models and tests—but also runs and verifies the full test suite plus a manual reproduction of the user’s scenario. Transcript 1 sketches the code change but never integrates or validates it against the tests.

Transcript 1 walks through the repository, locates the upstream fix commit, applies the precise change in `Catalog.__iter__`, updates the CHANGES file, adds a regression test, and fully verifies that all gettext tests pass. Transcript 2 only applies the code change without updating documentation or tests and lacks thorough validation. Transcript 1 therefore demonstrates the rigor and completeness of the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is far more thorough and accurate: it explores the full repo, identifies the exact upstream fix commit, updates both the source code, CHANGES file, and adds the regression test exactly as upstream, and verifies the changes end-to-end. Transcript 1 only patches the code in isolation without updating tests or changelog.

Transcript 1 performs a deep investigation of Sphinx’s AST‐based signature parsing and the util.inspect code, identifies both root‐cause issues, constructs a precise patch, adds new tests, runs the full test suite and end‐to‐end builds, and summarizes the changes. Transcript 2 is much briefer and only sketches a partial fix without test coverage or verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper investigation of both the AST-unparsing and signature-parsing pathways, methodically tracing defaults from the AST through `signature_from_str`, padding defaults properly, and exhaustively verifying via unit tests, end-to-end builds, and linters. Its fix handles all edge cases and integrates new tests cleanly, reflecting a more thorough and robust debugging process.

Transcript 1 provides a complete fix by applying the upstream patch, resolving CHANGES conflicts, updating deprecation docs, usage docs, tests, and verifying no regressions. Transcript 2 scopes only code and usage‐doc changes and omits updating CHANGES and deprecated APIs.

Transcript 1 walks through locating relevant code, precisely implements the upstream patch—including adding `merge_members_option()`, updating `option_spec`, adjusting filtering logic, deprecating the old merge function, updating docs and tests—and verifies behavior with tests. Transcript 2 only inspects code without applying changes.

Transcript 1 shows deep repository exploration, pinpoints the exact bug (`split(None, 1)` vs. `rsplit(None, 1)`), locates the upstream Sphinx commit, applies and tests the patch, and summarizes the minimal change. Transcript 2 is more ad hoc, less precise, and makes unnecessary attempts before arriving at the same fix.

Transcript 2 quickly locates the upstream Sphinx fix for issue #9224, cherry-picks and applies the precise one-line change (`split`→`rsplit`), updates the changelog and tests matching the official patch, and verifies against the full test suite. Its approach is more direct, shows knowledge of Sphinx’s git history and release process, and is more concise and correct.

Transcript 1 is significantly more thorough and knowledgeable: it locates the precise upstream commit, cherry-picks it, applies the minimal patch, updates tests and changelog, and then runs end-to-end verification including HTML rendering. Transcript 2 applies a more superficial find-and-replace without full context or comprehensive testing.

Transcript 1 cleanly locates the `object_description` implementation, adds the enum branch, runs localized tests and verifies the fix end-to-end without unnecessary detours. It shows clear understanding of Sphinx internals and addresses the issue directly, whereas Transcript 2 spends extra effort hunting for upstream commits and environment quirks.

Transcript 1 exhibits a far more comprehensive, robust implementation: it defines extensive modular helpers (including grid‐based concavity checks and stable segment integrals), enforces log‐concavity at multiple stages (with both slope monotonicity and point‐above‐hull tests), and includes a 23‐test suite covering end‐to‐end distribution checks, input validation, non‐concave rejection, and internal module tests. Transcript 2 is correct but less thorough in both log‐concavity screening and testing.

Transcript 1 delivers a clean, end-to-end implementation with modular helper functions, thorough log-concavity checks, and a comprehensive test suite that passes on the first run without any trial-and-error or code corruption. Transcript 2 repeatedly stumbles over environment and code-generation issues (e.g. missing Python, messy Perl edits) before finally regenerating the file. The smooth, correct execution in Transcript 1 reflects the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic, using both constraint- and score-based searches, detailed CI tests, BIC comparisons, introspection of pgmpy’s classes, correct parameter fitting via LinearGaussianBayesianNetwork, exact intervention with pgmpy’s do/simulate API, and thorough validation. Transcript 2 takes a more ad hoc, error-prone approach (manual regressions with incorrect CPD construction, simplistic CI checks) and lacks the depth and correctness of Transcript 1.

Transcript 2 demonstrates more advanced use of both constraint-based (PC) and score-based (Hill-Climbing with Gaussian BIC) structure learning, rigorous model validation (covariance matching, BIC comparison of 6-edge vs. spurious 7-edge), and comprehensive use of pgmpy’s built-in do‐operator and simulate methods with cross-checks. Its deeper validation and use of high-level API features indicate a more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a more systematic and robust approach: it cleanly installs and uses the HuggingFace datasets library, inspects the dataset schema and counts domains correctly, filters by domain, checks for missing values, and accurately tokenizes with the specified tokenizer. Transcript 2 shows more trial-and-error, manual file exploration, and a small inconsistency in concatenating tokens. Thus Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more systematic and robust approach—verifying domain-to-source mappings, checking for missing values, using the `datasets` library’s filtering, and maintaining an explicit plan—whereas Transcript 1 relies on simpler assumptions and raw parquet reads without such thorough validation.

Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model—it dives deeply into the custom libstdc++ patches, uses gdb watchpoints, objdump, inspects symbol layout, forms and discards partial fixes, and ultimately delivers a fully verified solution with exhaustive Valgrind and output-diff checks. Transcript 2 reaches a similar fix but with a far more cursory analysis and testing.

Transcript 1 provides a deep root-cause analysis, extracts and reads the patched libstdc++ source, correctly identifies the facet registration bug, and implements a precise workaround in user.cpp that forces library-internal facet registration via ostringstream before the custom heap is installed. Transcript 2 also diagnoses the issue but initially attempts wrong fixes (inline has_facet) and only later converges to the correct ostringstream approach after extensive missteps. Transcript 1 is more clear, direct, and correct.

Transcript 1 provides a far more thorough, systematic solution: it exhaustively verifies the differential characteristic, builds and tests the attack in simulation, documents the attack in detail with clear explanations, and performs extensive end-to-end testing across many key instances. Transcript 2, while correct, is briefer, less documented, and performs more limited testing.

Transcript 1 presents a clear, correct differential characteristic (0x80800000→0x02000000), validates it, and then succinctly implements and tests an efficient filtering attack. It avoids the missteps and extra debugging seen in Transcript 2 and delivers a precise, well‐structured solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper cryptanalytic approach—deriving exact linear relations in the FEAL G-function, chaining multi-round linear trails with probability-1, and staging a sub-million-operation C attack that runs in 0.1 s. Transcript 2 settles for a meet-in-the-middle brute-force scheme on 2²⁰ × 2²⁰ states. Transcript 1’s detailed analysis, efficient use of linear cryptanalysis, and rigorous verification mark it as the more capable model.

Transcript 1 presents a concise, mathematically grounded meet-in-the-middle attack using the invertibility of F, clean Python prototypes, hash tables to reduce complexity, and thorough verification. Transcript 2, by contrast, resorts to sprawling C code with nested loops and ad hoc staging that is far more cumbersome.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper, more methodical analysis—inspecting git history to recover the original validation logic, tracing through helper functions and multi-dicts, verifying the patch with both automated tests and manual sanity checks, and providing a structured summary. Transcript 2, while correct, is more cursory and lacks the thorough provenance and validation steps shown in Transcript 1.

Transcript 2 demonstrates deeper analysis by tracing the missing validation through the Git history, reinserting the original control-character checks, performing manual runtime tests to confirm the fix, and providing a structured summary of the vulnerability, fix, and verification. This level of thoroughness and validation indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 exhibits a more structured, robust approach: it maintains an explicit deployment plan, checks for configuration overrides, implements a clean deployment hook (wiping targets before checkout), measures and verifies push-to-deploy latency, and even resets the repo to a pristine state for a final smoke test. Transcript 2, while functional, is less thorough in environment validation, cleanup, and robustness.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more thorough, structured approach with explicit planning, robust cleanup and reset steps, advanced hook logic (clean deploy via directory wipe), custom SSH_ASKPASS handling, detailed TLS and HTTP status verification, and resetting the repo to a pristine state exactly matching the test specification. These systematic checks and resilience measures indicate a higher level of capability.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a more systematic, end-to-end verification: it checks the environment, handles service generation, implements comprehensive client tests (including missing keys and negative values), asserts correctness, and even verifies the open port. Transcript 2 is more cursory, uses fewer tests, and has incomplete port verification.

Transcript 2 performs more thorough environment validation (checking Python and pip versions), uses more comprehensive client tests (including negative and missing‐key cases with assertions), verifies package versions and port availability, and provides a clear final deliverables summary. This greater rigor and completeness indicates it was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and rigorous: it derives minimal macros, measures keystrokes, validates allowed commands, restores the original file, and runs full- and partial-size end-to-end checks. Transcript 2 is looser, slower, and skips detailed compliance checks. Thus Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a deeper overall analysis and optimization: it rigorously verifies the uniform input format before choosing a simpler, lower-keystroke macro sequence, restores the original input file for clean testing, and conducts multiple end-to-end performance and compliance checks. Its solution is both more keystroke-efficient (49 vs. 76) and significantly faster (∼71s vs. ∼156s for the full run), showing superior capability.

Transcript 1 shows a deep, end‐to‐end solution: building and tuning a custom C/C++ extension, exhaustive fuzz testing, handling corner cases, auto‐rebuild logic, and achieving 6–25× speedups. Transcript 2 simply wraps LAPACK via SciPy for a modest 1.5–2.5× gain. Transcript 1 is clearly the work of the more capable model.

Transcript 2 goes far beyond invoking SciPy’s LAPACK wrapper by authoring a complete C/C++ extension with balancing, Hessenberg reduction, Francis QR, and inverse iteration, plus extensive fuzz-testing, adversarial cases, and build-flag tuning to achieve 6–26× speedups and zero correctness failures. Transcript 1 merely leverages scipy.linalg.dgeev for a modest 1.5–2.5× improvement.

Transcript 1 systematically analyzes the cost model, derives theoretical lower bounds, and implements a dynamic-programming optimizer with Lagrange multipliers to jointly trade off cost, latency and padding. It then carefully tunes parameters, validates all metrics, and achieves near-optimal results. Transcript 2 resorts to a series of ad-hoc heuristics and brute-force gap tuning without the same principled optimization.

Transcript 1 methodically explores the data, iterates through multiple heuristic and DP-based strategies with code-driven evaluation, and arrives at fully validated batching plans meeting all constraints. Transcript 2 stops mid-optimization and never delivers complete, validated plans.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and systematic: it inspects environment details, reads Mailman workflow source to understand confirmation semantics, carefully configures Postfix and Mailman, diagnoses and fixes a subtle mbox ownership bug, and writes and runs both the provided and extended end-to-end tests successfully. Transcript 2 is much more error-prone and disorganized, with misconfigurations and unsupported settings requiring repeated trial and error.

Transcript 2 is more structured and efficient, using built-in tools like postconf and runuser, writing concise scripts, and debugging only where needed, whereas Transcript 1 resorts to lengthy manual file rewrites and repeated trial-and-error. Transcript 2 demonstrates clearer planning and more precise commands.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It maintains a clear plan, deeply analyzes the examples programmatically to infer the correct period-3 mapping, resolves merge conflicts with a well-documented, robust implementation, and performs extensive verification including randomized generalization tests and cleanup. Transcript 2 arrives at a correct solution but with a more superficial merge resolution and only minimal example testing.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more systematic and robust approach—using an explicit planning tool, exhaustively validating hypotheses (testing multiple periods, including p=2 and p=4), and performing 200 randomized generalization trials and cleanup—whereas Transcript 1, though correct, is less thorough in validation and organization.

Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model—it implements arbitrary‐precision in C, robustly parses and validates input, and exhaustively tests both the C and Python paths (even downloading and sandboxing the exact Python 3.12.3 runtime and cross-checking large outputs). Transcript 2, while eventually functional for small inputs, settles for 64-bit arithmetic, struggles with polyglot quoting, suppresses warnings hackily, and runs only basic tests.

Transcript 2 delivers a far more sophisticated solution—writing a full arbitrary-precision BigInt Fibonacci in C, orchestrating isolated Python 3.12.3 installs, and exhaustively testing both Python and C halves across thousands-digit inputs—whereas Transcript 1 stops at an unsigned-long-long implementation. Transcript 2’s depth and thorough validation mark it as the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far deeper level of system inspection and robustness: it implements a pure-Python ISO reader to extract kernel and initrd when mounts aren’t available, customizes the boot command line for serial console, daemonizes QEMU with a PID file and monitor socket, and writes a full Telnet negotiator to reliably detect the login prompt. Transcript 2 takes a more straightforward approach without handling these edge cases.

Transcript 1 delivers a concise, robust solution: it launches QEMU directly with a telnet‐serial console, gracefully handles missing tools, and uses a simple Expect script to wait for the login prompt. Transcript 2 massively overengineers the task—writing a full ISO9660 parser and manually extracting kernel/initrd—despite the ISO already supporting serial console logging.

Transcript 1 shows a clear plan, implements the regex, and then exhaustively validates it with both core and edge‐case test suites (including performance checks) by adapting to the available Perl environment. Transcript 2, by contrast, struggles with environment issues, provides only limited testing, and lacks the same level of rigor and coverage.

Transcript 1 clearly builds and validates the full solution—handling IP and date boundaries, enforcing “last date” via a negative lookahead, and exhaustively testing dozens of edge cases despite tool limitations. Transcript 2 offers a simpler pattern that never enforces “last date” and tests far fewer scenarios.

Transcript 1 shows a far more thorough, robust solution: it implements full file/directory/symlink scanning, uses SHA-256 checks, preserves modes and timestamps, handles oversized files at newline boundaries, compresses the manifest, and includes extensive automated testing on real and synthetic data. Transcript 2 is correct but simpler and lacks many of these capabilities.

Transcript 2 is more capable—it not only implements sharding and tree‐fanout but also round‐trips file modes, mtimes and symlinks, splits oversized files at newlines when possible, gzips a versioned manifest (with support for chunked manifests), and includes exhaustive testing of edge cases and failure modes. Transcript 1 is solid but lacks metadata preservation and some of the richer error‐handling and generic edge‐case support found in Transcript 2.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it systematically inspects the environment, correctly maps every RStan hyperparameter to PyStan/httpstan arguments, installs the required C++ toolchain, writes and verifies the Python script, runs sampling, handles warnings, and provides a clear, complete summary. Transcript 2 is more error-prone and disorganized, requiring multiple debugging iterations and lacking the concise, structured presentation of the final result.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper level of expertise by inspecting PyStan’s internal APIs, mapping `init_r` to `init_radius`, digging into httpstan’s argument parsing code, and carefully resolving compilation issues. Transcript 2, while correct, is less thorough in its investigation and debugging.

Transcript 1 is significantly more systematic and robust: it inspects the environment, handles missing tools, verifies checksums, updates a clear plan, confirms instrumentation flags in the Makefile, and comprehensively tests the build, coverage data, and PATH setup. Transcript 2, by contrast, is more ad hoc, misses checksum verification, has installation missteps, and provides less thorough validation.

Transcript 2 is clearly from the more capable model—it structures the work with an explicit plan, verifies the source checksum, inspects and confirms build flags, and performs thorough end-to-end validation (including login/non-login shells and `gcov` smoke tests). Its methodical updates, deeper verifications, and cleaner organization demonstrate higher capability than the more ad-hoc, trial-and-error approach in Transcript 1.
